description_full: WSFS Financial Corporation operates as the savings and loan holding company for the Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB that provides various banking services in the United States. It operates through WSFS Bank, Cash Connect, and Wealth and Trust segments. The company offers deposit products, including noninterest-bearing demand deposits, money market, and interest-bearing demand deposits, as well as certificates of deposit and jumbo certificates of deposit. It also provides loans, such as commercial and industrial loans, commercial mortgage loans, and construction and land development loans, as well as residential and consumer loans comprising residential mortgage, equity secured lines and loans, installment loans, unsecured lines of credit, originated education loans, and previously acquired education loans. In addition, the company offers ATM vault cash, smart safe and cash logistics services, planning and advisory services, investment management, and personal and institutional trust services. WSFS Financial Corporation was founded in 1832 and is headquartered in Wilmington, Delaware.

financial_summary: WSFS Financial Corporation is a mid-cap financial services business with a $4.0B market cap on $1.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 23% against a 9% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $214M in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.77× cash conversion.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 8.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
